content:
PRs #44120 and #44189 have generated some discussion regarding appropriate usage of docs#IsMulCommutative in place of docs#CommGroup within the group theory library.

In some situations, docs#IsMulCommutative seems basically unavoidable:

  1. iff lemmas such as center G = ⊤ ↔ IsMulCommutative G or IsMulCommutative (G ⧸ N) ↔ commutator G ≤ N
  2. commutativity of a subobject as a hypotheses such as IsMulCommutative H → IsMulCommutative (H.map f)

But for other situations either option is viable:

  1. commutativity of a subobject as a conclusion such as IsMulCommutative (center G) (could instead be CommGroup (center G))
  2. commutativity of a type as a conclusion such as IsMulCommutative (G ⧸ commutator G) (could instead be CommGroup (G ⧸ commutator G))
  3. commutativity of a type as a hypothesis such as IsMulCommutative G → IsSolvable G (could instead be CommGroup G → IsSolvable G)

In short, the group theory library has many predicates (solvability, nilpotency, etc..), and using docs#IsMulCommutative as a predicate for commutativity is potentially convenient (especially with the iff lemmas). But the counterpoint is that replacing docs#CommGroup with docs#IsMulCommutative in cases 3, 4, and 5 is simply moving from bundled to unbundled with all of the associated downsides.

Relevant thread from earlier this year on usage of docs#IsMulCommutative for subojects: https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/287929-mathlib4/topic/commutativity.20of.20subobjects/with/579041327

Pinging @Xavier Roblot, @Sébastien Gouëzel, and @Jireh Loreaux.
What happens if we add the instance Group G → IsMulCommutative G → CommGroup G?
docs#IsMulCommutative.instCommGroup is scoped in the IsMulCommutative namespace for performance reasons, I think
My advice on the PR is to use IsMulCommutative only for subobjects (because that's the point of the design), and activate the IsMulCommutative scope in files where this is relevant.
I think 3 and 4 should be CommGroup and 5 should be IsMulCommutative (the weakest-hypothesis, strongest-conclusion paradigm)

I like the unbundled versions, unless performance takes a hit (#new members > Purpose of Std.Commutative, etc. classes @ 💬).

I don't like the fact that CommGroup instances create diamonds, even if they're implicit_reducible so it's technically fine. It's also strange that what should be a commutativity theorem has to be a def with data.

To have bundled stuff has been a design choice in mathlib from the start, for performance reasons. Given the size of the library, I don't think it would make sense to change the design now, especially since we have a perfectly good workaround (only use IsMulCommutative for substructures, and activate the instance in contexts where such substructures arise).

I'm not a big fan of switching to unbundled just in this specific corner of the library, for coherence throughout Mathlib.
But something a priori can only be a group (e.g. Galois group), in that case the only viable option is IsMulCommutative.
Sure, if you have a group which is constructed by some other means, and then a theorem that this group is commutative, then you can formulate it with IsMulCommutative.
I agree with everything Sébastien Gouëzel has said here.

If some were to run an experiment deleting all Comm... classes in favor of IsMulCommutative, and to our surprise there were a performance boost (or even if it were neutral), I'm rather sure we would jump on it.

Jireh Loreaux said:

I agree with everything Sébastien Gouëzel has said here.

Just to clarify, does this mean that (3) should be IsMulCommutative (subobjects) and (4) and (5) should be CommGroup (types)?

Sébastien Gouëzel said:

only use IsMulCommutative for substructures

If IsMulCommutative is only for subobjects, should it be changed to only accept a MulMemClass?
There are other usages where IsMulCommutative is needed (e.g., iff lemmas, and galois groups)
... and if we want to state some field extension L/K is an abelian extension, we can only say [IsMulCommutative Gal(L/K)]. There are no other viable ways.

Thomas Browning said:

Jireh Loreaux said:

I agree with everything Sébastien Gouëzel has said here.

Just to clarify, does this mean that (3) should be IsMulCommutative (subobjects) and (4) and (5) should be CommGroup (types)?

I would expect (3) to be CommGroup (because it's always commutative). IsMulCommutative is for subobjects which may or may not be commutative depending on context. Note that there is Subgroup.commGroup_isMulCommutative to guarantee that you can still use it to relate to other subobjects via IsMulCommutative.

But yes, I would expect (4) and (5) should be CommGroup too.

Jireh Loreaux said:

Thomas Browning said:

Jireh Loreaux said:

I agree with everything Sébastien Gouëzel has said here.

Just to clarify, does this mean that (3) should be IsMulCommutative (subobjects) and (4) and (5) should be CommGroup (types)?

I would expect (3) to be CommGroup (because it's always commutative). IsMulCommutative is for subobjects which may or may not be commutative depending on context. Note that there is Subgroup.commGroup_isMulCommutative to guarantee that you can still use it to relate to other subobjects via IsMulCommutative.

But yes, I would expect (4) and (5) should be CommGroup too.

I am a bit surprised with that answer. What's wrong with (5) when commutativity is an hypothesis? I don't see what we gain by making docs#Group.instIsSolvableOfIsMulCommutative use CommGroup rather than IsMulCommutative
Just coherence throughout Mathlib: all lemmas assuming that a group G is commutative are spellt with [CommGroup G], so let's keep this pattern everywhere we can.
This seems to me to be a lemma about groups that happen to be commutative, rather than a lemma about commutative groups, so I think it should be spelt with IsMulCommutative

IsMulCommutative isn't for groups that happen to be commutative, it is for subgroups that happen to be commutative. Think of it this way: when will that lemma apply (if it takes CommGroup as a hypothesis)? Either there is some relatively concrete group G which is commutative, in which case you should definitely have created a CommGroup instance for it, or you're dealing with an abstract commutative group, in which case you should be assuming CommGroup G, or you're working with a subobject that happens to be commutative, in which case you should have the IsMulCommutative namespace open and then your IsMulCommutaive subgroup gets upgraded to a CommGroup anyway.
You could also have a quotient that happens to be commutative, rather than a suboject. This is not uncommon in group theory.

E.g., you have a group G, and a subgroup N, and you know that N and G/N are abelian (e.g., maybe you know commutator G ≤ N), and you want to deduce that G is solvable, so you need to know that G/N being abelian implies G/N is solvable.
Yeah, but in that case I would still argue that this is about subobjects (because you're quotienting by one) so you should have IsMulCommutative open.

Jireh Loreaux said:

IsMulCommutative isn't for groups that happen to be commutative, it is for subgroups that happen to be commutative.

So are you in favor of #mathlib4 > Usage of `IsMulCommutative` @ 💬?
this would leave us without a way to say that a certain group isn't commutative

No, because then you lose the CommGroup G → IsMulCommutative G instance, which allows you to automatically use theorems for the latter when you have the former. IsMulCommutative is morally used for subobjects, not literally about them.
@Aaron Liu, I thought Jireh just said that it shouldn't be used for groups.

Jireh Loreaux said:

No, because then you lose the CommGroup G → IsMulCommutative G instance,

You would have [CommGroup G] (S : Subgroup G) : IsMulCommutative S and [Group] (S : Subgroup G)[IsMulCommutative S] : CommGroup S, which would remove the need for any local instances / scopes

Junyan Xu said:

I think 3 and 4 should be CommGroup and 5 should be IsMulCommutative (the weakest-hypothesis, strongest-conclusion paradigm)

I agree with this except for when defining instances, we should prefer the bundled hypothesis.
I guess simp lemmas should also prefer the bundled hypothesis.

Jireh Loreaux said:

IsMulCommutative isn't for groups that happen to be commutative, it is for subgroups that happen to be commutative.

Again, Gal(L/K)?

Eric Wieser Right, but I think what I'm claiming is that sometimes, but rarely, you need IsMulCommutative G for G : Type, not G : Subgroup H. For example, I think this is probably the correct approach for docs#IsCyclic.isMulCommutative or docs#IsKleinFour.isMulCommutative. Otherwise if we used CommGroup here, when G is a Group and Lean wants to know if it's a CommGroup, it would search for IsKleinFour G and IsCyclic instances. Maybe that's okay? But it seems suboptimal to me.

In addition, to Aaron's point, without IsMulCommutative for types, we lose the ability to say that a particular group is non-commutative. Or otherwise to have ↔ statements for commutativity of a group (e.g., IsMulCommutative (Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) ↔ n ≤ 2). Of course, we even with a statement like this, there should often be a corresponding CommGroup instance for the situations in which it is applicable.

Jz Pan said:

Again, Gal(L/K)?

indeed, this is fine:
Jireh Loreaux said:

IsMulCommutative is morally used for subobjects, not literally about them.

There are going to be situations in which IsMulCommutative is the only spelling available, in which case using it is fine.
I argue that things like docs#Abelianization.lift are misspelled though.

And then some theorem requires CommGroup but not merely Group + IsMulCommutative, so in this case in order to use such theorems, one always need open scoped IsMulCommutative to get the instance IsMulCommutative => CommGroup.
I think that is the system working as intended.

Jireh Loreaux said:

IsMulCommutative isn't for groups that happen to be commutative, it is for subgroups that happen to be commutative. Think of it this way: when will that lemma apply (if it takes CommGroup as a hypothesis)? Either there is some relatively concrete group G which is commutative, in which case you should definitely have created a CommGroup instance for it, or you're dealing with an abstract commutative group, in which case you should be assuming CommGroup G, or you're working with a subobject that happens to be commutative, in which case you should have the IsMulCommutative namespace open and then your IsMulCommutaive subgroup gets upgraded to a CommGroup anyway.

Perhaps I have a construction which in general gives me a not necessarily commutative group, and then I want to apply it to a special case for which I know the group is commutative (this is the case with Gal(L/K), for example).
I think I just addressed this: when it's the only spelling available, it's fine.

But in this case, I would need this extra step to use this theorem, which is morally about general groups that satisfy the additional property of commutativity, and not about commutative groups. There are many other lemmas which fall into this category as well.
so I think this view should be reflected in the signature of the statement, as [Group G] [IsMulCommutative G], instead of [CommGroup G] (which looks like it is a lemma about commutative groups)

Jireh Loreaux said:

I think that is the system working as intended.

Indeed, I think I'm understanding the system as intended now. The question is just whether the system is best serving these situations in group theory that are more about groups that happen to be abelian than about CommGroups.

Aaron Liu said:

so I think this view should be reflected in the signature of the statement, as [Group G] [IsMulCommutative G], instead of [CommGroup G] (which looks like it is a lemma about commutative groups)

I have just asked it a few minutes ago, and the conclusion is that we have to open scoped IsMulCommutative.

Thomas Browning said:

The question is just whether the system is best serving these situations in group theory ...

Certainly unbundling, in group theory as in many other places throughout the library, would be more natural in many ways (especially if we could have the dream scenario where writing CommGroup G just unfolds syntactically or similar to Group G + IsMulCommutative G), but we have historically not taken that approach for performance reasons, and so we take our lumps.

As I said upthread, if someone wants to run an experiment where we unbundle commutativity everywhere throughout the library so we can see the performance impact, I'm open to it, but I won't do it myself. I would be rather surprised if performance improves, or even stays neutral.

Jireh Loreaux said:

As I said upthread, if someone wants to run an experiment where we unbundle commutativity everywhere throughout the library so we can see the performance impact, I'm open to it, but I won't do it myself. I would be rather surprised if performance improves, or even stays neutral.

Just ran it in #44466. Total build time is up +0.40% which is less than I was expecting.

Cool! Maybe it's possible to find shortcut instances that could even improve that, by investigating the costly places

Also looking at the lints, it also uncovered lots of places with unused commutativity assumptions!
e.g. docs#Matrix.fromBlocks_eq_of_invertible₁₁
Although many of these are technically because it generalized defs to non-commutative structures, e.g. docs#Matrix.charmatrix / docs#RingHom.IsIntegral, which isn't always desirable.
This happened because unlike theorems, defs don't include section variables that they don't need.
Could you avoid such cases by adding the section variables explicitly to the defs?
I wonder if it'll make the performance better or worse
